passage.title: Equality, Justice and Human Rights
paras: After the Second World War, the world had seen what happens when governments decide that some people matter less than others. In 1948 the United Nations agreed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Its first article says: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'

Equality means treating everyone the same: the same rules, the same rights, the same chances. It is the idea behind one person, one vote, and behind the law that says no one may be refused a job because of their race or religion.

But treating everyone the same is not always fair. Equity means giving people what they need so that they can have the same chance. A pupil who cannot see the board needs to sit at the front; a building needs a ramp so that a wheelchair user can enter. Equity does not give some people more rights; it removes the barriers in their way.

Rights on paper are not enough. In George Orwell's Animal Farm, the animals' first commandment is 'All animals are equal'. By the end it has become 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.' The words survive, but the fairness behind them is gone.
A fair society therefore needs both: equal rights for everyone, and the will to make sure those rights are real for everyone too.
